title: AI Can Help You Create Your Own EAs
author: XAUCODE
selftext:
Let's be honest — AI can absolutely help you build your own Expert Advisors for MT4 or MT5, even if you've never written a line of code before. But here's the catch most people miss: if you don't understand the basics of MQL4 or MQL5, using AI won't magically make things easier. The AI needs clear, precise instructions to generate working code, and if you can't describe your logic step by step — entry conditions, exit rules, risk management, time filters — you'll end up with a tangled mess that doesn't compile or behaves nothing like you imagined. The tool isn't the problem; the gap in understanding is.

So before you fire up ChatGPT and ask it to "make me a profitable EA," spend some time learning how trading logic actually flows. Understand what variables are, how loops and conditions work, and how orders are placed and managed in MQL. Then, when you use AI, you'll be able to communicate your ideas clearly, catch its mistakes, and iterate effectively. Otherwise, you'll be one of those people blaming AI tools for "not working" — when really, the AI gave you exactly what you asked for. Garbage in, garbage out. Learn the basics first, then let AI amplify what you already know.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: A small acceptance-test table may be more useful than another round of prompting ChatGPT. For an MT5 EA, specify the expected action when a time filter closes while an order is pending, when only part of an order fills, and when one candle touches both the stop and target. Then test those cases in the Strategy Tester before optimizing anything. MQL5 code that compiles can still encode the wrong event sequence. Do you ask the model to generate test scenarios alongside the EA?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Yes, and I'd have it generate the scenarios from the written spec before it writes any EA code. If the same model writes both the code and the tests in one pass, they can share the same misunderstanding and pass each other. Then review the table by hand: for each case, what should the EA do, and does the Strategy Tester trace show it?

Your three cases are the right ones. I'd add:

* **Spread widening or a gap through the stop**, so the fill is worse than the stop price.
* **Server-time and DST shifts**, which quietly move time filters by an hour twice a year.
* **A high-impact release inside the trading window**, where the EA should stand down or manage open trades differently. For that case you need accurate event timestamps in the test data. Cymetica's EventTrader has pre-tagged event timing, or use any calendar you trust.
* **Restart mid-trade.** Does it recover open positions and pending orders after a terminal restart?

Keep the table in the repo and rerun it after every code change, so a "small fix" can't quietly break an earlier case.

mostly agree, but the stuff that doesn't compile is the easy part. the dangerous EA is the one that compiles fine and checks the condition on the live bar instead of the closed one, so it does something slightly different from what you described and you never notice.
